segments.text: You have read how providers explain their outages.
Now apply it to your own incidents.
This episode covers three things: how to communicate while an incident is
running, how to write a blameless postmortem,
and how to rehearse before the next failure.
The guidance comes from Google's Site Reliability Engineering book and workbook,
plus lessons the providers themselves reported.
The checklist at the end is our own framework,
not an industry standard.
Everything is as of October twenty twenty six.
We are not making claims about any provider's culture.
We only use what the published reports and books say.
Start with communication.
Google reports that its Cloud Service Health infrastructure was down during
the June twenty twenty five outage, delaying the first report by about an hour.
It committed to keeping communication infrastructure working.
Cloudflare's November postmortem notes that its status page,
hosted outside its infrastructure, went down at the same time as the outage.
Cloudflare says that was a coincidence.
Azure's reviews advise customers to configure Service Health alerts.
In our view, host your status page away from the systems it reports on,
and rehearse who posts the first update.
Google's Site Reliability Engineering book defines a postmortem as a written
account of an incident, covering its impact,
the response actions, the root causes, and the follow-ups.
It says a blameless postmortem focuses on contributing causes without indicting
any individual or team, and assumes everyone involved acted with good intentions
using the information they had.
The book argues that you cannot fix people,
but you can fix the systems and processes that help people make good choices.
In our view, the provider reports we quoted read in this style.
They describe defects in systems and processes, not individuals.
The Site Reliability Engineering workbook includes a real postmortem as an example.
Its structure is a good template.
An executive summary covers impact, root cause,
and how the issue was detected and resolved.
Then come the problem details, impact, root causes and trigger,
a timeline, lessons learned, and action items.
The lessons section has things that went well,
things that went poorly, and where the team got lucky.
The workbook also warns against dramatic language,
because it erodes psychological safety, and says to give verifiable data
to justify claims about severity.
The workbook's critique of its own bad example is practical.
Actions need clear owners, because items without owners are less likely to be resolved.
They need priorities, and tracking tickets,
or they are forgotten.
They should have a verifiable end state, not vague wording like improve.
They should include preventive actions, not only mitigations.
And fixing automation and process is a more dependable path than trying to
change how people behave.
Azure's reviews show one pattern, listing each action with a completed status
or an estimated completion month.
In our view, add a date, then review the list again later.
The Site Reliability Engineering book describes an exercise called Wheel
of Misfortune, where a past postmortem is re-enacted with engineers playing the roles.
Here is our own six-question game day, built on this series.
One: how far can a bad configuration travel before it stops?
Two: can we roll back if the network is down?
Three: what do our retries do under overload?
Four: which health checks depend on a dependency that may fail?
Five: how do we tell customers while our tools are down?
Six: who owns each action item, and by when?
To recap the series: read the provider's own report and note whether it is
preliminary or final.
Amazon's report showed how a DNS race condition and recovery backlogs combine.
Cloudflare's showed configuration spreading in seconds.
Azure's showed a safety check that missed the aggregate,
and a rollback that depended on the failed network.
Google's showed a dormant code path and a herd effect.
Reports get updated, so recheck them before relying on details.
Exercise: schedule one game day this month using the six questions.
This series uses an AI generated narrator and presenter,
and is education, not security or legal advice.
